newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK Telecom sees FCC rates plan opposed.
newsitem.headline: HK Telecom sees FCC rates plan opposed.

text.p: Hong Kong Telecommunications Ltd on Wednesday predicted wide opposition to U.S. proposals to slash international call settlement rates, saying Washington was trying to solve U.S. woes on the backs of foreign carriers.

Keith Bernard, Hongkong Telecom's director of regulatory affairs, said the company would file comments arguing against the U.S. Federal Communications Commission (FCC) proposal to set "benchmarks" on fees carriers pay each other to terminate calls.

"The way we envision this, (the FCC plan) is literally a proposal that will transfer profit from foreign carriers to U.S. carriers," Bernard told reporters. "We are fundamentally opposed to any unilateral action."
"We have heard from quite a few other carriers who have similar concerns that we do," he added. "A number of other countries are already raising objections with the FCC."
The settlement rate regime needed to be improved, but multilateral was the way, Bernard said.

The FCC proposed in December to cap the fee foreign telecom carriers charge U.S. carriers to complete U.S.-origin calls at 15, 19 and 23 U.S. cents per minute for high-, middle- and low-income countries.
The FCC argued that while the average cost to complete a call is no more than nine cents, settlement rates tend to be five to 10 times costs, forcing U.S. callers to pay too much.
U.S. carriers also originate more calls than they complete, so they have to pay more settlement fees than they get, with the outflow expected to hit US$5.5 billion this year, the FCC said.
Comments on its proposals are due next week with the FCC's replies to be filed by mid-March.
The stakes are high for Hongkong Telecom.

The U.S.-Hong Kong settlement rate currently is about 47 cents per minute. With seven times more calls coming from the United States to Hong Kong than going the other way, analysts expect Hongkong Telecom to net more than US$200 million in fees this fiscal year.
But Hongkong Telecom said the FCC's arguments hold no water.
Keith Harrison, the company's director of international, said the seven-to-one imbalance in U.S.-Hong Kong traffic was the direct result of call backs, a business the FCC encouraged.
With a call back service, a Hong Kong-to-U.S. call is automatically bounced back as a U.S.-to-Hong Kong call and charged at U.S. rates.
Through another system called refile, a Hong Kong-to-Venezuela call turns into two U.S. origin calls.

While incoming and outgoing traffic traditionally used to grow in parallel, in the past 18 months incoming traffic hardly grew at all while outgoing traffic has skyrocketted, reflecting the growing popularity of call back, Harrison said.

Lower settlement rates were not guaranteed to mean lower consumer rates since while global settlement rates are already on a downtrend, rates U.S. carriers charge consumers for international calls are on an uptrend, he added.
Bernard also said the US$5.5 billion U.S. carriers pay foreign firms was misleading as it said nothing of international revenues U.S. carriers kept, which were steadily rising.

He said settlement fees were also a sovereignty issue since authorities in many territories, Hong Kong included, had policies of using international revenues to subsidise domestic service -- policies the FCC proposal could unilaterally hamper.
Bernard said while international opposition to the FCC proposal was likely to be strong, he did not know what Hongkong Telecom would do if the U.S. regulator went ahead.

"We're hoping in fact it doesn't come to that, that the commission will see the light and defer and take their effort into the ITU (the UN's International Telecommunications Union) to try to solve the problem there," he said.
